subtopic: ATLANTIC COAST-PROPOSED IMPROVEMENTS IN SERVICE

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: ATLANTIC COAST-PROPOSED IMPROVEMENTS IN SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 6 the hon. Member for Queens-Lunenburg asked me if I would be in a position to say something about the urgent need for larger and properly equipped coast guard ships on the east coast. I indicated I hoped to make a statement very shortly. This statement is a little longer than an appropriate answer to a question, so I thought I should make it on motions.
The statement is regarding an increase in the facilities and equipment of the Canadian Coast Guard of the Department of Transport for marine search and rescue work in Atlantic waters.
General co-ordination of search and rescue activities is the responsibility of the Department of National Defence which has established search and rescue co-ordination centres for this purpose. Traditionally and by law, all vessels available, whether owned by the Government or privately owned, must assist when needed under the direction of the search and rescue co-ordination officers. At the search and rescue co-ordination centres the Canadian Coast Guard provides special marine advisers to assist in matters relating to marine operations. In addition the Coast Guard some years ago put into service three small and five medium sized cutters solely for the purpose of providing search and rescue competence and doing general patrol work in this connection. Two of the medium sized cutters, which were designed for coastal and sheltered waters work rather than either deep sea or close inshore work, have been stationed in the Atlantic area.
As a result of continuing study of requirements in the Atlantic area, it has been decided that the Canadian Coast Guard capability will now be expanded by the provision of four large new cutters, possessing full capabilities for deep sea work. These cutters will be approximately 200 feet in length and will cost around $4 million each to build. They
will operate primarily in the offshore areas frequented by our deep sea fishermen.
In addition, to meet conditions in which neither the large nor medium sized cutters can operate, several shore based lifeboat stations will be developed. It is planned to develop five new stations of this sort in addition to the one that already exists in the Bay of Fundy. The Canadian Coast Guard will provide the lifeboat, but it is intended that the manning will be based on the voluntary part time support of the local community, possibly somewhat similar to the system which applies in Great Britain. These lifeboats will cost about $150,000 each.
No decision has as yet been taken on the location of the lifeboat stations. Further field investigation will be necessary, including consultation with local groups as to how best the voluntary type of organization mentioned can be set up under Canadian Coast Guard supervision.
The full implementation of the program which I have mentioned in Atlantic waters will probably take four to five years. It will do a great deal to strengthen and improve our ability to provide patrol and assistance for search and rescue work not only in our immediate coastal waters but even farther afield, and will be of great benefit to fishermen and other marine operators in the Atlantic provinces as well as to international shipping.
Similar studies of requirements with regard to both the Pacific coast and the Great Lakes are to be carried out to see what further expansion of Coast Guard capabilities in these areas is required.
I should emphasize that it is not intended that the provision of these vessels should in any way imply that marine rescue should become solely a Government responsibility, or should weaken the prime responsibility for rescue at sea which traditionally and in law is a matter of mutual help among seafarers of all kinds.

AMENDMENT RESPECTING DURATION OF A PARLIAMENT
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-107, to amend the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1964, (duration of House of Commons).

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING DURATION OF A PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING DURATION OF A PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
It has long been my contention and it is, I think, the contention of many members of the Canadian public that elections should not take place every year or so in the federal field. This bill would provide, with certain safeguards and guarantees, for a four year term. It would mean that the responsibilities of Government could be exercised by any Government which had the support of the House of Commons, except in extreme emergency. Provision is made for the amendment of the British North America Act which now limits the duration of a Parliament to five years so as to allow, with some exceptions, four year terms free of elections and free of campaigning in the House of Commons.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: REMOVAL OF ANTI-MISSILE SYSTEMS FROM JOINT U.S.-CANADIAN CONTROL

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REMOVAL OF ANTI-MISSILE SYSTEMS FROM JOINT U.S.-CANADIAN CONTROL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I see that the Minister of National Defence is back in his seat, so I wonder if he would answer the question I asked the Prime Minister in his absence on Tuesday, relating to the two anti-missile systems which are to be removed from joint Canadian-U.S. control and put under sole United States control. Can he bring the House up to date and report on this matter; or perhaps the Prime Minister has the answer?

May 27, 1965
Inquiries of the Ministry
Hon, Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence): Mr. Speaker, consultations between the Canadian and United States Governments on all matters affecting their joint interest in the defence of North America is at all times full and effective. The Canadian Government has been aware of the development of the weapons systems referred to in the press. I may say at this point that this is not a removal, as stated in my hon. friend's question, but is a matter of assignment.
The assignment of forces to the operational command of NORAD has been and remains a matter for national decision. In accordance with this arrangement the systems referred to are a national, defensive measure by the United States to make provision for countering possible threats from orbiting satellites. These systems were at no time assigned to NORAD.
There is absolutely no basis for the speculative suggestion that this is indicative of any decline in support on the part of either Government for our joint NORAD command. Although the requirements of North America defence are changing with the development of new weapons, both offensive and defensive, Canada and the United States will continue to co-operate closely to provide jointly and effectively for the defence of the continent.

subtopic: REMOVAL OF ANTI-MISSILE SYSTEMS FROM JOINT U.S.-CANADIAN CONTROL
speechtext: In view of the developments to which the Minister has just referred, can he say if he considers that the usefulness or future usefulness of NORAD is coming to an end?

speechtext: I would not say so, Mr. Speaker. It could be that in time there may be changes in the relationship due to changes in weapons systems. Nevertheless there will continue to be a requirement for close cooperation and co-ordination between the two countries as there has been in the past.

subtopic: REMOVAL OF ANTI-MISSILE SYSTEMS FROM JOINT U.S.-CANADIAN CONTROL

moment in respect of the stations on the Pine Tree Line, which are the important ones remaining, that there is every indication these will be continued in operation for some time to come, perhaps a number of years.

speechtext:

First of all, in respect of private funerals, officers and men may request and receive time off from their duties to attend and participate if they wish, either in or out of uniform. Attendance and participation, however, are on a strictly voluntary basis. In the case of official military funerals, details of servicemen may be required to attend and participate, as authorized by the Department of National Defence. In the case of official military funerals, the practice continues to be for the casket to be suitably draped with the national flag of Canada.

speechtext:
The House resumed, from Wednesday, May 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Knowles, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Olson:
That this House recognize the need for improving its procedures to provide full opportunity for the critical examination of proposed legislation and to ensure the effective dispatch of public business;
That this House agrees upon the need for allocating the time for the business of the House; and
That, in order to secure improved examination of the details of legislation and of public spending, while maintaining the full authority of the House, this House agrees upon the value of making increased use of Standing Committees;
That this House accordingly orders:
1. That detailed examination of estimates, saving always the right of the Committee of Supply, be undertaken by Standing Committees and that not more than 36 days of the time of the House be allocated to the business of supply in each session. For the purpose of this order, the business of supply shall consist of proceedings on motions "That Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair"; supplementary or additional estimates for the financial

year; interim supply; and main estimates whether for the coming or the current financial year. That a Special Committee of the House, consisting of twenty-two members, to be designated later by the House, be instructed to prepare and to submit to the House forthwith the changes in Standing Orders consequential upon this order, including any means of giving to the opposition an opportunity to select the departmental estimates to be discussed.
2. That the Standing Orders be amended by adding thereto a new Standing Order 15-A, to read as follows:
Standing Order 15-A
15-A. (1) There shall be a Business Committee to which the leader of each party in the House from time to time by written notice to the Speaker may appoint one member.
(2)	During routine proceedings a Minister of the Crown may request that the question of allocation of time for consideration of any item of business or stage thereof be referred to the Business Committee for consideration and report, and upon such request being made such question shall stand referred to the committee.
(3)	The Business Committee shall report back to the House on or before the third sitting day following such request.
(4)	If the Chairman of the Business Committee reports that the committee has unanimously rec-commended an allocation of time for the item of business or stage thereof, a Minister of the Crown may without notice propose a motion, to be decided without debate or amendment, for concurrence in the report, and if agreed to, the motion shall have the same effect as if it were an order of the House.
(5)	If the Chairman of the Business Committee reports that the committee has been unable to reach a unanimous agreement or if the committee fails to report within the time specified by Section (3) of this Standing Order, a Minister of the Crown may give notice that at the next sitting of the House he will move that an order be made allocating the time for the item of business or stage thereof.
(6)	A motion of which a Minister has given notice under Section (5) of this Standing Order shall be made during routine proceedings. Unless the debate on the motion has been previously concluded, Mr. Speaker shall at fifteen minutes before the expiry of the time provided for Government business in such sitting interrupt the proceedings and forthwith put every question necessary to dispose of the main motion. A motion requesting allocation of time, if agreed to, shall have the same effect as if it were an order of the House-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take part in this debate because of the extreme importance of the subject matter. It is important for more than one reason. It is important because this is one occasion when Parliament can do the nation a service by clarifying in the minds of many people what we are trying to do and what this resolution really proposes.
We have read and heard a great deal from commentators in the press, on television and on radio, and have heard a great deal of discussion in other circles about the need for reforming Parliament. Many of these statements in my opinion are loose and unjustified. One only reforms something that is delinquent, and I do not believe this institution is delinquent in respect of any important matter.
Parliament is representative of all the people, and I suppose the people feel they can justifiably criticize Parliament as much and as often as they like because they believe in reality they are criticizing themselves. This is to some extent true because Parliament is a reflection of the people of Canada.
This criticism of Parliament is not limited to outsiders. A great deal of criticism has been levelled at Parliament by the press and others, and in many cases one would almost think the writers had never so much as paid a visit to Parliament. That is not representative of the press generally. Many very fine editorials and comments have been made in the press on this subject, and I refer particularly to the lead editorial in the Montreal Gazette of yesterday.
Much of this criticism is made by the Members of this House of Commons, and I notice that the most extreme views expressed in respect of the so-called reform of Parliament usually emanate from Members of this House with the least parliamentary experience. As time passes those Members gain a greater insight into the functions of Parliament and the history of our present rules.
Yesterday the Minister of Transport, with his usual frankness, admitted that after having been a Member of the Government, as a Member of the Opposition he learned a great deal in that role in regard to the rules of Parliament. I believe that to be a true state-
May 27, 1965

House of Commons Procedures ment if only because he made it, and I congratulate him for his frankness in this regard. It is noticeable, however, that he is one of a small minority of individuals in the Government or, for that matter, on that side of the House, who has had the advantage of that experience.
I note in the proposals put forward by the Government an almost fatal attraction for equating the improvement of Parliamentary procedure with a limitation on freedom of speech and the freedom of Opposition members to criticize the Government. There is a need for rules which result in the expeditious handling of matters which come before Parliament wherever that is possible, but I do not believe that expedition in itself is of tantamount importance. The preamble to the resolution states:
That this House recognizes the need for improving its procedures to provide full opportunity for the critical examination of proposed legislation and to ensure the effective dispatch of public business;-
That is a very high-minded statement, but the Government proposals which follow that preamble are equated with this most desirable objective, and thereby attempt to trick someone-perhaps the public-into equating whatever is proposed with reform and expedition. I do not agree that in this case that would be the result.
We find ourselves adopting axioms based on assumptions that are not only incorrect but cannot be proven to be correct and, in many cases, can be proven to be false. I think we should get down to the fundamentals and in this context attempt to determine what is important and what should be reformed. The opposite to improvement, of course, is deterioration; and I think it can be established, or at least argued, that some of the suggestions put forward in this motion would represent a deterioration of the proceedings of Parliament rather than an improvement, and retrogression rather than reform. They would result in a corruption of some of the fundamental rules of our House.
We as Canadians are virtually united in one respect. That is, we are proud of our democratic system and the type of freedom we enjoy under our parliamentary system. We may, however, fall into several errors by assuming that the institution of Parliament itself is that which provides the freedom we enjoy. It does not follow that if a country has a Parliament of some sort it enjoys all the freedoms and liberties to which we are accustomed. For example, in Russia-and I

do not think too many would like to live under that system-they have a Parliament. Of course in Russia they do not have an opposition. Some individuals assume that if a country has a constitutional election all the freedoms we enjoy will be safeguarded. I believe I am correct in suggesting that the Nazis came to power in pre-war Germany as the result of a constitutionally carried out election, at least in the first instance. These are not the things that safeguard our freedoms which are fundamental.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I should like, in this connection, to quote briefly from Beauchesne's fourth edition, page 55, where I find these words:
A minority party may question ministers, may criticize but cannot control in the ordinary case a Government with a reasonably large majority. There can be no control of the Executive where the supporters in Parliament are prepared without question to obey the leaders of their party- through the Whips. All that the minority party-the Opposition-can do without support from members of the majority party is to question, inquire and criticize, but whilst this does not amount to control it is an important method of checking abuses of power.
With the support of a majority of Members it would be possible for a Cabinet to suspend the sitting of Parliament, have the minority members arrested, withdraw the safeguards of liberty such as Habeas Corpus and freedom of speech, and to establish virtually a dictatorship. All this, too, could be done within the law. It is surprising how few members of the general public appreciate how uncontrolled the Cabinet is where it has the support of a loyal majority in Parliament and that "the supremacy of Parliament" in this sense is absolute and subject to no real safeguards of any kind. We may add that the majority of the House of Commons does not always represent the majority of the electors in the country. It often happens that, owing to the redistribution of electoral districts, a party may come out of the general elections with a majority of elected members without having received the majority of the votes given by the electors who went to the polls or whose names are on the electoral lists. That party may form a Cabinet, but the official Opposition together with other anti-ministerial groups, though sitting to the Speaker's left, are the real representatives of the people; and their right to challenge by legitimate means every measure or proceeding sponsored by ministers cannot be disputed. In such case, when the House divides, members who oppose the Administration may act on behalf of the majority while Government supporters represent the people of Canada.
This, as has been pointed out, can be true when a government party has a clear majority in the House of Commons. It is even more true when they form a minority government. I do not want to leave the impression that having an opposition, in itself, is sufficient to guarantee the freedoms of our democratic
May 27. 1965	COMMONS
system, to which we have become accustomed. We must not only have an opposition, an alternative to the present government, but an opposition must be untrammelled in its freedom to criticize and see that the government is held responsible to the people who elected it for its conduct of the nation's business.
Again, I find a very apt quotation in Beauchesne, page 78. This is the statement made:
The "Official Opposition" is a standing proof of the British genius for inventing political machinery. It has been adopted in all the Dominion Parliaments; the lack of it is the chief weakness of most of the Continental systems... It cannot be denied that under modern conditions the concerted action of the Opposition is the best means of controlling a Government-by criticizing defects in administration loudly enough for the public to take notice. This is not a particularly pleasant, if salutary, experience for ministers, and it is only natural that they should be tempted to think both that the Opposition abuse their opportunities and that their opportunities are unnecessary ample. The facilities which the Opposition enjoy for initiating criticism on subjects of their own selection are dependant on technical forms and Parliamentary conventions. The share of the time of the House which the Government puts at the disposal of a body whose raison d'etre is to show up the mistakes of ministers and eventually to turn them out of office- this share of time, which during the last fifty years has not fallen below a quarter of the effective days of the session, is worth more interest-than it usually receives. The least that can be said is that since it is only through the Opposition that some measures of Parliamentary control survives, the uninterrupted respect for the rights of the Opposition which contemporary governments have shown should be accepted as prima facie evidence of the soundness of their Parliamentary faith.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in my judgment our democracy, as we recognize it, requires not only respect, as we know, for the rules as they exist, but it requires that a government, even with a large majority, must recognize that minorities have rights. They must recognize that they are responsible not only to the people who voted for them and elected them, but they are responsible to all citizens, and that they are actually holding in trust the traditions of freedom and liberty which have been the keystones in our country's history. They must hold themselves always ready to be accountable to the people for their actions and their administration of public business.
Of course, when any overt attack is made on our system it is plain for everyone to see. When we are threatened by such things as military conquest or subjugation by force, the issue is clear for us. There has been a wealth of treasure spent and tremendous sacrifice in our lifetime in defence of our 22620-111

We are not sufficiently on guard against the steady decline in our freedoms. We might, by an unintentional striving for efficiency or some other goal just as inconsequential, lose our basic rights and freedoms as a people.
Now people, in any phase of human activity, naturally try to rationalize their failure. They try to blame it on somebody else. A government, when it fails to make progress in getting its own legislation approved, if it has not achieved the goals in the amount of time it expected, rationalizes this failure. It is human nature for governments to do it, and of course the obvious whipping boy is the rules of the House, and the fact that in their judgment the opposition are going beyond reasonable criticism. Now, anyone who is criticized, I suppose, believes that his critic goes beyond reasonable bounds of criticism; that is human nature. Our system as it is built and has evolved is designed for the purpose of not allowing any individual who may be in a position of power, whereby he can be corrupted by that power, to subjugate the public interest to his own desires. So periodically we have governments blaming the rules for what they consider the slowness of parliamentary procedure.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Committees to revise the rules were appointed in 1913, 1927, 1953 and 1955, and each time they substantially curtailed debate in an endeavour to shorten sessions; but each time they failed. My contention is that if these present proposals are adopted in their entirety -I hope they will not be, although there is much in them acceptable to everyone in the House-they would fail in their purpose. In addition they would curtail and impinge upon some of the historic freedoms of parliament.
Always, of course, a great deal of this type of thing is done in the name of reform. I point out that many words in our language have been brought into disrepute by misuse of them. Any time the U.S.S.R. speaks about world conditions it talks in terms of the peoples' democracies that wish for world peace. It perverts both the word democracy and the word peace until they are almost meaningless. The same is true of the word reform.
It is almost inevitable that when some body wishes to propose something unpalatable it speaks of it as reform, and that has special application to this Government. Its Members'
1724	COMMONS
House of Commons Procedures philosophy is based on the assumption that misuse of language is beneficial to their interests, and that a great many gullible people can be led into believing that anything they do is an improvement and is in itself a reform.
No doubt many Members of the Government belong to the Reform Club. I would not be a bit surprised if Lucien Rivard belongs to it too; but the fact that that is its name does not give it any special merit. By the same token, if you call a thing reform, that is not good enough: You have to substantiate that it is reform.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext:
The selection of good or bad should not be made on the basis of what is old or new, but on a more objective basis. We often hear the term "the effective dispatch of public business." For example, in the preamble to this resolution we find the words, "and to ensure the effective dispatch of public business." This is misleading because parliament's chief role is not to dispatch public business. That is the job of the executive; that is the responsibility of the Government. That is what it is there for, to dispatch the public business; and Parliament is chiefly here to examine the Government's performance. Another reason is to give the executive additional powers if it is considered to be in the public interest that that should be done.
Over the years there has been a tremendous trend to give the executive more and more power by adding a great list of legislative items in every session of parliament. In many cases much of this legislation, is not only unnecessary, but is detrimental and should be more carefully scrutinized by government before placing it in front of parliament.
No doubt this stems from the public's belief that a government's merit is in direct proportion to the amount of legislation it stuffs through parliament; but in my judgment this has little to do with the merit of a government. It is something which stems from the T.V. age in which we live, where in election campaigns all parties-and this is human
[Mr. MacLean (Queens) .1

nature-make grandiose promises of what they will do in the way of stuffing legislation through parliament if they become the next government.
It is possible to have a tyranny of a majority that is just as bad for a country's interests as any other kind of tyranny. Because a group of people happen to constitute a majority-and in this case they are not even that, they are a minority-it does not give them any divine attributes which make them always right. There must be a finer realization; there must be some rights accorded to minorities as well. Again I turn to Beau-chesne because this is summed up very nicely there, at page 55:
In every country attempts have been made to ensure that there shall be some check on the powers of the majority. Lord Bryce said In "Modern Democracies": "That a majority is always right, i.e. that every decision it arrives at by voting is wise not even the most fervent democrat has ever maintained seeing that popular government consists in the constant effort of a minority to turn itself by methods of persuation into a majority which will then reverse the action or modify the decisions of the former majority."
Decision by majority is not an absolute and unquestionable principle. "Our constitution, to use Burke's phrase, is something more than a problem in arithmetic." There is no divine right of a mere numerical majority any more than of King's. Majority decision is a measure of convenience essential to the dispatch of business, the result, "of a very particular and special convention, confirmed by long habits of obedience." The idea that a majority, just because it is a majority, is entitled to pass, without full discussion, what legislation it pleases, regardless of the extent of the changes involved or of the intensity of the opposition to them, the idea in fact that majority edicts are the same things as laws, is wholly alien to the spirit of the constitution.
As I have already said, I believe the main trouble is that we have been subjected to government by propaganda; the notion has grown up that expediency is the main virtue; and the more stuff parliament passes the better parliament it is. I do not share that viewpoint. Parliament has a great obligation to examine everything on its merits and it is quite conceivable that on occasion parliament is at its finest when it refuses to pass legislation proposed to it. In this connection I have one more brief quotation I should like to give:
One of the main functions of the House consists in debating public Issues, a function which can only be filled by complete freedom of speech. There will always be contests between groups and parties, minority and majority, and, in the debates that follow, the rules of procedure are all-important. Delays, multiplicity of amendments and even obstruction must not always be regarded as illegitimate public weapons.

The privilege of freedom of speech enjoyed by Members of Parliament is in truth the privilege of their constituents. We do not seek this privilege on our own account. It is secured to Members, not for their personal benefit but to enable them to discharge the functions of their office without fear of prosecution, civil or criminal. I think this should not be forgotten. This motion that when a' subject has been considered for a certain length of time it should pass automatically is one of which I do not approve. I cannot see any logic in it. I think it would be just as sensible for us to say in our courts of justice that if a conviction cannot be brought against an accused person in two days he should automatically be discharged. Member for Vancouver-Burrard has outlined the details, the directors and sponsors of the bill as well as the financial position of the Laurentide Bank of Canada. He has described it as a bank which would be based on the West Coast, namely Vancouver, B.C., but also with offices in Montreal as well. He described it as a private bank which has a charter to operate on a national basis, a bank which being headquartered in British Columbia could better serve the interests of individuals and industries, all prospective developers of Canada's western economy.
I trust that this House, faced with the passage of this bill, can deal with it in short order and that there will not be undue opposition from other corners of the House. I trust that the case of these Canadian
May 27, 1965

citizens, who are prepared to launch a bank in Western Canada, will be heard, and their right to be cross-questioned by Members of the House, will be realized in the Banking and Commerce Committee shortly.

subtopic: LAURENTIDE BANK OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take part in the debate on Bill No. C-95, an Act to incorporate Laurentide Bank of Canada, and it is with pleasure that I support the amendment moved by my colleague from Charlevoix (Mr. Belanger) to postpone for six months the consideration of this bill.
Several hon. members have spoken on this subject and it makes one wonder whether it is really necessary to grant new charters to Canadian banks. I maintain that we should wait until the Bank Act has been revised, in order to ensure greater justice toward the provinces. In fact, I wonder why we should grant a charter to the Laurentide Bank of Canada, owned by a few shareholders and other associates, who practically all are directors of other already existing banks.
I realize that banks have given tremendous help to the Canadian consumers and having two banks more or less would not alter the competition much, since they are all regulated by the same legislation already.
If the Senate had not refused to accept the proposals made by the government of British Columbia, we would have been more inclined to adopt this measure. But in view of the statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) to the effect that it was extremely risky to allow a provincial government to invest in a bank, I must say that we are stumped there because the provincial banks represent the interests of each and every citizen in a province. In that case all the people, and not only a handful of individuals, are represented in that bank or hold shares in it.
That is why I say the Minister of Finance should reconsider his statement. Since he is supposed to be intelligent, he should sit down and realize once for all that the whole population of a province should be entitled to hold shares in a provincial bank.
Furthermore, a provincial bank could bring revenues to a province, and this would enable the authorities to reduce taxation which at present is a crushing burden.
Private Bills
Mr. Speaker, when will this end; indeed at the present time we are encouraging loans which will allow an individual to get deeper into debt. As a matter of fact, we are going into debt at a catastrophic rate, and some are wondering when there will be an end to the great danger which the financial system represents for this country.
Mr. Speaker, it is no more dangerous to let provincial governments invest in banks than it is to let individuals do so because the promoters of the Laurentide Bank of Canada all have personal interests to look after.
If the Bank of Canada played its primary role in the field of finance in Canada, we would have nothing against the multiplication of charter banks so long as the latter confined themselves to the provision of services in the field of loans, exchange and administration of the Canadian economy. Then the banks could be most helpful to individuals. As things stand now, such is not the case, however. The banks control credit in the country and that is what we, Creditistes, cannot accept because at present the banks have the privilege of creating credit, even with the guarantee of the borrowers and the government and are thus playing part of the role of the Bank of Canada, the creation of the money required for the consumption of goods and services in the country.
As the people's representative in the house of commons, it is my duty to delve into facts and to bring out the truth concerning the financial system of the country and to work toward the removal of the causes of the permanent doldrums in which our financial system is entangled and continues to bog down, year after year, even though the Minister of Finance goes to great lengths to try to prove that Canada is very prosperous.
No, Mr. Speaker, Canada is not prosperous Most Canadians are not prosperous and it is up to us, members of parliament, to see to it that this situation which is becoming every day less bearable is corrected.
But the one who is responsible for this situation, is the Minister of Finance, who, on many occasions, has given signs of incompetence and unwillingness.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Inasmuch as we have the labour force and the materials available, if the government would only assume its responsibilities as regards finance and the creation of new credit this would mean a great change in the living conditions of certain classes of people.

May 27, 1965
Private Bills
Instead of making gifts or loans, without interest, of $200 million to other countries, it would be much wiser to use similar amounts of money in this country so as to solve the unemployment problem in Canada, and especially in the province of Quebec where it is more serious. The unemployment situation is really terrible, and in the case of representatives of constituencies like mine which are largely inhabited by working people, it involves a dreadful amount of extra work. We are required to be present in the house, but whenever we are not in our ridings to settle numerous cases relating to social assistance and unemployment assistance, we are blamed, and I think this is perfectly normal.
That is why I would endorse a parliamentary reform which would allow every member to spend in his constituency at least two or three weeks every four or five weeks in order to meet the needs of the population. Now, all that is due to a lack of credit, to unemployment and to a tremendous lack of industries. It is a well known fact that in Quebec we need 200 to 300 new industries in order to employ the available labour.
Therefore, the job of the member of parliament is made very difficult if he wants to discharge his duties both in the house and in his constituency.
Last Tuesday I should have liked to be here at 2.30 p.m. but a family head was starving with his eight children and the social service refused to do anything before two weeks, so I had to go myself to the office to settle this case. And there are hundreds of such cases.
I said on severaT occasions and I repeat that if there is a lack of leaders, it is because we did not give our educators the necessary financial assistance to enable our young people to look forward to a better future.
We have juvenile delinquents, young people who do not know what to do. Why? Because they are unemployed; they cannot earn an honest living, so they wander in the streets and do not know what to do with themselves. This is why we are having trouble with them. If they were given the opportunity, to work, juvenile delinquency would disappear in our great country, Canada, which is supposed to be so prosperous and so rich.
If the Bank of Canada lent money to the provinces and municipalities at the administrative cost to build modem community centres, juvenile delinquency would quickly disappear.

Our Canadian families are being crushed under a burden of debts and by the exorbitant credit terms legally imposed by finance companies. That is why we have warned the people not to fall in the trap set by those finance companies who are exploiting them. With the interest they are charging on loans, under the present system, people have no choice but to come into the world surrounded by debts and to leave it on the instalment plan in order to get a decent burial. In between, they have to go through the expense of getting married, raising a family, buying a house and some furniture. There is no other alternative for them than to go to the banks who, most of the time, refuse to lend them any money and refer them to the finance companies, who charge more and whose directors are mostly the same persons. Mr. Speaker, this does not make sense. Banking is the most important matter that the government should consider because, in the long run, it is the banks that control the economic blood stream of the nation, and whoever controls credit, has the upper hand over the economic life blood of the nation.	.
When a country has a debt of $72 billion, or a per capita average of $4,000, I wonder where it is heading? It is high time to sound a warning note. Under the present system, we, members of parliament, should, before even considering the creation of other banks, take time out to consider the role which the Bank of Canada should play, for it is a most important one. When the Bank of Canada is authorized to create public credit for materials and the building of roads and schools, then we can think about creating more chartered banks and multiply them a hundredfold, if it is desired. It would no longer create a problem because chartered banks would then be playing their true role, which is to make credit available at a normal rate of interest, instead of rates as high as 24, 30, 35 per cent per year as charged today by finance companies. It is absurd and we believe that the number of chartered banks should not be increased Until the Minister of Finance becomes conscious of his role and of the authority he has over the Bank of Canada.
Recently, he admitted at least that the Bank of Canada came under his authority. When we are called upon to examine the budget, the first point to be considered will be the interest on the debt.
Mr. Speaker, we are paying more than a billion dollars in interest every year to
May 27, 1965

financiers and banks, and this is far from being normal. The country must be responsible for its credit and the creation of credit. Instead of paying those billions to a group of financiers, the money could be distributed across the country for useful purposes, to help the people and reduce taxes.
I still have on my desk a pile of letters with regard to income tax and charitable receipts which have been reduced to $200 and $225.
Who has all the bother? The members of parliament who have to look after those cases. But whose fault is it? It is the government's fault, because it is remiss in its duty. It is really shocking. And then people wonder why members are no longer interested in coming back to sit in the house. Indeed, a member who really wants to carry out his duties finds it very exhausting. If we are overworked it is due to the present system which is basically wrong.
I am against the establishment of this new bank so long as we fail to take the time required to look into the Bank of Canada Act. That is why I support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Charlevoix to give a six months' hoist to the bill so as to provide time to study the role of the Bank of Canada, to determine its function and its authority from a monetary point of view. Then, some thought may be given to the opening of branches throughout the country in order to extend credit.
The Bank of Canada must play its part. When the government needs money, it has a right to create a certain amount of credit. What does it cost the government? In a word, only the administrative cost.
But today, such is not the case; if the government wants to create money tomorrow morning, it has to kowtow to the chartered banks, to beseech them for a certain sum of money so that it may carry out its work, so that it may have credit of some kind.
Mr. Speaker, suppose a disaster should strike the country tomorrow morning; suppose there was a flood and that six provinces out of ten were flooded. For 10 to 15 days, the waters would subside; and then, what would the country do? Would we say: everybody is dead, the houses are destroyed, everything has been devastated, and that is the end of it? No. Credit would have to be issued for the reconstruction of the houses that have been destroyed and for the burial of the dead; credit would have to be created then.
Private Bills
If a war broke out tomorrow morning, there would be no question about finding the necessary money; credit would be created. But, for our unemployed, this seems to be impossible. This is utter nonsense. It is high time we should assume our responsibilities. People are waking up and they want to know who controls money in the country.
Some people are involved with exports and imports; a certain country cannot buy goods because it does not have American dollars, and so on. They should try to settle our own problems before tackling international ones. What I find most annoying in the House of Commons is precisely that 60 or 75 per cent of the questions asked deal with international matters when we are unable to settle our own domestic problems.
Mr. Speaker, I submit that we, members of the House of Commons, should assume our responsibilities because it is high time we sounded a warning note in matters of finance, and the problem has to be settled as soon as possible.

subtopic: LAURENTIDE BANK OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having met some of the representatives of the proposed Laurentide Bank, people who have a job to do-and I must say they are doing it-I still maintain my opinion concerning the possibility of having one or two banks in addition to our eight existing ones. I still maintain the position I took after listening to some of the arguments presented by supporters of this bill.
They argued strongly that the proposed bank will make money available more easily to small Canadian enterprises and individuals as compared with the trend of the big banks to make large loans to major companies.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Consider the latitude given to the eight existing banks, especially as a result of the reduction of the proportion of their reserves required for credit creation from 8 per cent to 7 per cent. Formerly the chartered banks were permitted to lend I2J times their reserve, or savings deposits, including Government bonds. Now the requirement has been reduced to 7 per cent, so they can lend 14.38 times the amount of their reserves. A few years ago they were able to lend 16 times the amount of their reserves, but that was in

May 27. 1965
Private Bills
wartime and the factor involved was the highest ever.
Would this proposed new bank really serve the needs of the Canadian people at the present time? I do not think so. What is needed is a change in our methods of financing in this country. I do not believe that one more bank, or ten more, or one less, would change the picture in any way. It is true that in order to accumulate some of this required reserve of 7 per cent the new bank might collect a few savings accounts. This is what happens when a new branch is set up-and I know what I am talking about. A number of depositors in existing banks or caisses populates close their accounts because they have been unable to get loans with individual managers. They open a savings account in the new bank and are granted loans. After a year or two when the operation becomes more stabilized in that branch, credit is restricted and a situation prevails similar to that which three or four years previously caused the new customers to transfer their accounts originally.
It is not by setting up additional financial institutions that we will help the Canadian people. We shall do that best by amending the law which applies to the Bank of Canada, permitting the Government to exercise more control over its credit. The Government may exercise control over the Bank of Canada to a certain extent in the fields of bonds and currency. But what about the credit created in each and every one of the branches of these chartered banks? It will not change this situation in any way to have one more bank making loans on the basis of a 7 per cent reserve.
If people close their accounts at the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce or the Bank of Nova Scotia and deposit them in the Laurentide Bank, what will happen? The lending powers of the other banks will decrease accordingly and the lending power of the Laurentide Bank will increase. Until we create sufficient real credit to balance the gross production of this country from time to time, it makes no difference whether we have ten banks, or 20 banks or 30 banks. The money deposited in current accounts does not matter, when it comes to the creation of credit. It is what is deposited in savings accounts that constitutes the reserve which can presenly be multiplied by 14.38 times in order to make loans to borrowers. There are now eight banks which lend on this principle.
Government bonds also constitute part of a bank's reserve funds. When I deposit $100 in

a bank, that bank can lend $1,438 on the basis of that deposit. It can collect the interest in respect of this sum. If the bank allows me 2j per cent or 3 per cent, how much does it collect on the $1,438 at 6 per cent, or 7 per cent, or 8 per cent. Some people may say the banks charge 6 per cent. I do not believe this. The rates start off at 6 per cent-I am talking now about a personal loan, when repayment begins at the end of the month. Toward the end of the repayment period, when most of the loan has been returned, the same rate of interest is charged despite the fact that the bulk of the money is no longer in the borrower's hands. Similarly, loans made by finance companies do not work out to 2 per cent interest monthly, as is sometimes advertised. By the time a borrower has finished repayment the rate has risen to 25 per cent or 30 per cent, or even more.
[DOT] (5:30 pjn.)
Someone may ask how I arrive at these figures. It is not hard when you consider that the Niagara Finance Company gives the borrower a note mentioning 2 per cent a month or 24 per cent a year. Of course there is a limit. It depends on how much you borrow. But it is 2 per cent a month for 12 months, or 24 per cent a year to start off. If that is not usury, it certainly is not far from it. In fact, to my mind it is legalized robbery. I don't give a hoot if you call it legalized permission to charge a higher rate of interest: it is still robbery.
When people are refused loans at the banks, they go to the finance companies and get their loans. Then the same notes are endorsed by the borrower and brought back to the bank, after the loan was refused by the bank in the first place. The loan is granted by the finance company, and when the finance company obtains the note, they go back to the bank and change it or have it accepted there. I asked one bank manager how it was that he accepted them when they came back from the finance company. He said, "They are guaranteed by the finance company". With what does the finance company guarantee these notes? They are guaranteed through the guys that borrow there. Good Lord, Mr. Speaker, if the finance company can guarantee the notes through the assets of its borrowers, why can't the bank do this in the first place? This is why you see some of the chartered banks giving more and more personal loans today.
Is the Laurentide Bank going to give us more purchasing power? No, Sir. The law does not change; it is exactly the same. It is
May 27. 1965

the same, whether the bank is there or not. The banks will not change their operations. The law permits them to operate in this way. And the law will not give us in this country any more banknotes, any more Government bonds, to act as a reserve for the banks. What would happen if a bank lent money beyond its reserves? The other chartered banks would lose money proportionately. This would not give the country any more credit. It might cut the other banks down in regard to their profit; but it would end up in the bank that went beyond its reserves anyway. The same people would be on the winning side, and the same people, the Canadian consumer, would be on the losing side.
This story of the big banks lending money to small enterprises, this story of the banks making personal loans to the individual consumer, is for the birds, Mr. Speaker. The proposed bank will not lend any more than the others do; it is the exact picture of the others. It is to be operated in the same way and under the same law, which permits banks to operate in this way. All banks will do exactly the same. They hand us all these flowers and make a beautiful window dressing. They can do that if they wish; but it does not change the picture underneath, because after a year or two years the proposed bank will have the same basic operations as the other banks.
It might be difficult for them to get this bill through the House, but have they ever thought of the Canadian consumer who goes every Monday morning to the kings of finance, the bank manager or somebody else? I do not blame the bank manager, because he has a job to do. He is a cog in a big wheel; and sometimes when I look at them going around like that it makes me think of this saying, "Blessed are those that go around in circles, for they shall be known as wheels". That is right, Mr. Speaker. The bank manager receives orders from above; he does his job. The clerks have to do their job. At the end of the day they make out their balance sheets at the branch and send it to the head office in Toronto or Montreal. There everything is compiled by electronic computers and they are able to say that the bank made so much profit or lost so much money. Where is the interest of the bank manager in all this? That guy is just a cog in the wheel. If that banker does not do his job, the cog is removed and replaced by a new one.
If we look back to 1936 or before that, the banker had to put his signature on a Canadian banknote before it was valid. That requirement has been removed. That was a
Private Bills
little more powder thrown into the eyes of the Canadian people; that was a little more window dressing; it was a little more mysterious. The banker does not have to sign them any more. But he has to do something. Mr. Speaker, I am sure you have a deposit in a bank. I am positive that if I have borrowed $100 from the same bank that conducts your financial affairs, your account does not go down by $100; yet I have borrowed $100 from that bank. You may say, "Yes; it is guaranteed by their reserves". Let me tell you something, Sir: A bank that is operating on the credit side is not making any money. I have noticed that. At one time I left one branch of the bank and my account was transferred to a new branch, and I noticed that the branch clearing was not the same; the two figures had been switched-the bigger balance was on the credit side. I asked the bank manager how the other branches were working on what you might call the debit side, and he said, "It is because we have more loans out at the moment than we have in deposits, and we are running under". I said, "How is it that the others were running over, or making a profit?" He said that some big banks were lending more, and you might have $2 million deposit in the savings department and $750,000 and $800,000 out in loans.
There is an advantage to being able to transfer, within the same bank, loans and things like that. But why not ask the chartered banks to lend what they have- no more, no less? You can't give what you haven't got; nobody can. How can they do it under a law passed by this Parliament? There is a reason for it, Mr. Speaker. If every Canadian citizen went out today and got the money that is in their savings accounts, retrieved it from the banks, you know what would happen. This was done with some of the banks, and they faced some pretty difficult times.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)

speechtext: Order. I am sorry but I have to interrupt the hon. Member because his time has expired.

subtopic: LAURENTIDE BANK OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think anybody can blame me for having talked too long on the bills to incorporate two banks and especially on this Bill No. C-95, to incorporate the Lauren-tide Bank of Canada, because this is the first time I have risen to speak on these private bills.

May 27, 1965
Private Bills
Lately resolutions have been brought forward and, in particular, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) introduced some bills concerning the monetary policy of the government or the Bank Act.
Recently we discussed Bill No. C-101, to amend the Bank of Canada Act, a measure concerning finance in this country. The house should also examine Bills No. C-102 and No. C-103 respecting chartered banks and savings banks in the province of Quebec.
We will soon be asked to approve or disapprove the renewal of bank charters which have to be renewed every ten years.
In regard to that legislation concerning the banks and the monetary policy, we have nothing definite, nothing specific, in short, no plan. We do not know where the government is headed for with its monetary policy.
During the discussion on Bill No. C-101, the Minister of Finance stated that he wanted to establish a monetary authority in the country and that in the event of disagreement or misunderstanding between the governor of the Bank of Canada and the federal government, the Minister of Finance would have jurisdiction and the authority to decide.
On the other hand, other resolutions have been introduced in the house. In fact, about a week ago, I put on the order paper notice of motion No. 27 asking the Minister of Finance to produce the written instructions of the present Minister of Finance and of his predecessors, the correspondence with the governor of the Bank of Canada since January 1, 1960.
I received the answer that those documents could not be tabled, because they were of a confidential nature. Then how can we control the monetary policy in this country?
How can we control this country's monetary policy if we do not know anything about the written instructions given to the governor of the Bank of Canada, if the authority in the field of monetary policy, that is the Minister of Finance, issues instructions on monetary policy to the governor of the Bank of Canada, and if, on the other hand, the members of parliament cannot take cognizance of such documents or instructions which exist or may have existed? Why submit to us bills designed to grant charters to new banks, if the present Canadian monetary policy is so confused that the government refuses to disclose to the members elected by the people the nature of our policy, the blue print of the monetary policy or the instructions the Minister of Finance has given in the past or will give in future to the Bank
[Mr. Rondeau.)
of Canada? On the other hand, in Bill No. C-103, page 31, section 63, it is provided that the savings banks in the province of Quebec shall maintain:
-15 per cent of such of its deposit liabilities as are payable in Canadian currency.
This means that savings banks in the province of Quebec will be allowed to make loans provided they have deposits amounting to 15 per cent, whereas the chartered banks- as the one to which it is intended to grant a charter at the present time-could, under the new amendment submitted recently, make loans while keeping a reserve of 7 per cent only. Why should one bank be required to maintain a 7 per cent reserve and another a 15 per cent reserve? If there must be uniformity in our monetary policy, that is the present financial set-up, why should the savings banks in the province of Quebec be required to maintain a 15 per cent reserve, whereas the chartered banks will be required to maintain a 7 per cent reserve only?
How can we say, in view of the situation of all these private institutions which are called banks, past or future, that we have a uniform monetary policy?
We have no objection to the granting of charters to new banks because we say that the country's monetary policy comes exclusively under the purview of the Minister of Finance, but we must know what this monetary policy is.
The Minister of Finance claims to be the master of our monetary policy, but he is unable to reveal what are those instructions, what is the plan, what is his policy; as an economist, as Minister of Finance, he should inform the Canadian people and the Canadian Parliament, because, if we do not know where we are going in the field of monetary policy, why should we incorporate new banks which will not tell us either where we will be heading for tomorrow?
Why has the monetary policy been left in the past to the whims of private enterprises called chartered banks? Chartered banks have but one purpose, and that is to lend the capital they have; shareholders want to make money by investing in banks and this is normal and logical, there is nothing wrong with that. On the other hand, we object to the granting of new charters to such banks, whether they are called Laurentide or Western or any others that may come about. If charters are granted today to those two new banks, how can we better control our monetary policy in the future?
May 27, 1961

As our monetary policy should come under the federal government, then we contend that credit, the creation of credit and the issuing of new money, should be controlled by the federal government. It does not matter if there are 8 or 80 chartered banks, the main thing is that they should only be empowered to lend whatever capital they have on hand; that would be normal. It is normal that shareholders, financiers, capitalists, all those people who have invested a million dollars in a bank would want to lend their million with interest, but we do object to the fact that those individuals are empowered to lend 92 and 93 million dollars more than their million, or are empowered to create credit. Creation of credit should come under the sovereign control of the federal government, of the state.
The individuals called bankers or capitalists, should be authorized to lend their capital, their money, and earn interest thereon, just as any individual interested in any company or just as any industrialist producing something should normally realize a profit. There is nothing wrong with the shareholders of a bank making a profit or earning interest on their capital. What is wrong is to give private businesses, banks in particular, the power to lend 12 or 14 times the capital they hold. We are surprised to hear the Minister of Finance tell us that the amendments contained in Bill No. C-101 will enable him, in the future, to exercise tighter control over the country's monetary policy, because although last year the banks were obliged to keep their reserves at 8 per cent, from now on they will be allowed to keep them at only 7 per cent. It means that the banks will have more power thanks to that new amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: LAURENTIDE BANK OF CANADA
speechtext: May I remind the hon. member for Shefford that he cannot discuss the amendment nor the substance of Bill No. C-101 to which he is referring at this time. I would ask him to come back to Bill No. C-95 which is now under consideration.

subtopic: LAURENTIDE BANK OF CANADA
speechtext:
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for reminding me that I was dealing with Bill No. C-101, but since all these bills have to do with the monetary policy and that even the proposed Laurentide Bank will be submitted to the requirements, the liberties or the freedom provided for in Bill No. C-101, an act to amend the Bank of Canada Act, I would consider that what I was saying was in respect to the Bank Act.
Private Bills
Mr. Speaker, we are requested to approve a new bank charter, and then instead of having eight, maybe we will have nine, perhaps ten in the near future, perhaps we will even have several others, and that is where we have an objection. We have nothing against potential, past or future shareholders in existing or future banks, we have nothing against them, because they are individuals who want a charter to make a profit. On the other hand, in the context of the Bank Act now in effect, we are against the granting of this charter by the federal government. Such a charter should be granted not in a rush, but normally, because the Bank Act grants a privilege, a power which would extend the existence of the financial system we have been criticizing for more than 20 years.
In the past we have never criticized banks as such, but rather the financial system which is responsible today for the fact that we have no control over the monetary policy of Canada, because banks are all-powerful in this country. In fact, they are private institutions which control the economic blood of the nation, and the federal government has no power over them. The government has powers in words, but none in fact. When the banks decide to restrict credit, to raise the interest rate or even to change the monetary policy of the country, it seems the federal government has agreed beforehand to all their requests. Why? Because they control the economic blood of the nation, which is very important.
We do not have the right to leave the economic blood of the nation in the hands of a few individuals because, sooner or later, because they control the economic blood of the nation, they will ruin the nation to the prejudice of the people.

subtopic: LAURENTIDE BANK OF CANADA
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: LAURENTIDE BANK OF CANADA
speechtext:
They may laugh about those assertions, but the fact remains that day after day our debts are increasing and to whose advantage? To the advantage of those who hold a bank charter. When we look at the public debt, we wonder who is buying the bonds issued by the federal and the provincial governments. Well, they are purchased by the banks with credit, figures and accounting; this is not money earned but money newly created in the form of figures. This is what makes the Creditistes say that the federal government should let the chartered banks keep on accepting deposits and lending that money to the public, to private

May 27, 1965
Private Bills
enterprise but that the federal government through the Bank of Canada, should control public credit, the monetary system, the financial system of the nation. Otherwise, the country will keep on going down hill, because in spite of all its legislation, the federal government is always restricted, always limited, is in a strait-jacket, is always conditioned by the money, the dollars of the nation's bankers because they are the ones who control the economic fate of the nation.
[DOT] (5:50 p.ra.)
A former prime minister of Canada, Mr. Mackenzie King, used to say: "Give me control over the credit of a nation and I do not care who makes the laws." He said that in Saskatoon in 1935 and he was absolutely right.
What he said in 1935 is even truer in 1965: When one has control over the credit of a nation, one does not care who makes the laws. That is the reason why, if the Canadian government really wants to have authority and fight poverty, it must not give more scope to chartered banks while requiring a smaller reserve.
Who created poverty? It is our present banking system. It is the banking system we know that makes people poor. Give even more charters to banks, without amending the Bank Act, and you will multiply the number of poor people in Canada. The same causes result in the same effects.
We have handed over our monetary policy to some individuals who can get the country deeper and deeper into debt day in and day out, year in and year out, from one war to another and from one crisis to another, and who are sufficiently powerful to bring about prosperity during wartime and crisis during peacetime. Then, why issue new bank charters? So that, depending upon their aims and ambitions, they can impoverish at will a greater number of people?
Mr. Speaker, we do not object to a new charter, but we object to the powers which this new charter will grant those individuals. It is quite normal that banks lend money with interest; but it is not normal that banks, with a capital of $7 can lend $100. This means that they can lend $93 which they do not have and on which they charge interest. This is blue ruin. Our present financial system is a cancer and, if we in Canada, are not ready to fight this cancer, it will destroy our great and rich country, because the greater the number of chartered banks with powers we know are theirs and the greater the number of bankers able to lend more

money than they own, the faster we shall travel on the road to ruin.
It is often said that with money you can control everything and that money means power. But the less money banks have, the more power they get, because until now they could grant loans while maintaining an 8 per cent reserve fund, and now they are to be authorized to maintain a reserve of 7 per cent only. That will give the lie to the old saying: with less money, you would not have any rights at all.

speechtext:
I should like to repeat the two questions I put to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) yesterday. The right hon. gentleman was sympathetic toward the points I raised but I do not see that any consideration has been given to them.
The first concerns what should be done when committees report to the House. It seems to me this is a fundamental question which should be dealt with by Standing Orders. Nevertheless it seems to have been overlooked in the amendment which the Minister of Labour has put forward. If there is a desire to limit debate as far as possible in order to afford more time to debate other subjects, it seems foolish, after a particular committee has reported, to deal with the subject matter of the report rather than with what is contained in the report itself. If a debate does not take place on a committee report after it has been tabled, it seems to me that the sittings of a committee become nothing more than a high class educational program for the benefit of the Members who take part. These committees should be recommending procedures to improve the operations of the various departments, or ways of bringing about economies in expenditure. If these recommendations were brought before the Committee of Supply there would probably be a short debate and the Government would have to decide whether to adopt the recommendations or reject them. If it rejected them it would have to explain why it did so. I think this is an obligation owed by the Government to Members who would otherwise waste a great deal of time in committee. Attendance on these committees is like taking a short university course on a particular subject in the parliamentary field. Of course, it tends to make the Members experts-sufficiently expert to be able to come back into the House and "rag" the subject to death for two or three days if they wished.
The second point which I put to the Prime Minister and to which he gave a favourable reply was the suggestion that these various committees be set up according to a timetable so that neither the Government nor Opposition parties could drag their feet as they did last year. Every time a responsible Minister was asked why a particular committee had not been set up he told the House that the Members had not yet been named by all the parties in the House. I think a time limit should be imposed by standing order, prescribing the date by which the various committees should be constituted.
May 27, 1965

I do not insist that effect be given to these proposals right now. But I will say that if the Government is not willing to consider them it is unlikely that much success will be attached to the changes in the rules which are now proposed, because no fundamental change will really have been made. These two points have always seemed to me to be important. In studying the procedure in Great Britain I found that before doing anything else the committees usually considered carefully what action had been taken as a result of the recommendations previously made.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
If there has been no result, that again becomes a matter of discussion. I believe the matter of setting a time, so that the Government is not faced with getting the co-operation of all parties in the committee, can be established and should be something taken care of by our Standing Orders. Mr. Speaker, I think all parties in the House have indicated their interest and desire in streamlining the rules of Parliament so that the business of this House can be carried on in a more efficient and effective manner. I also think that through the debate that has taken place up until this point the independence of the Speaker has been foremost in the minds of all hon. Members, and more especially in the minds of the Opposition, so as to ensure that their rights are jealously guarded. Because they, in effect, are guardians of the freedom and protection of the people against the actions of the executive. Surely, Sir, what we as Members of the Opposition must be certain of before we agree to any rule changes is the protection of our rights and the right of any individual in this House, whether he be a backbencher or a frontbencher, to be able to rise in his place on the appropriate occasion and bring before the House his views on matters of national and local concern.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) argued that the proposal for a permanent Speaker must be foremost in the minds of all hon. Members if we are to consider adequately rule changes proposed by the Government which will greatly curtail the activities of the Members of this House. They must have the complete assurance of an
May 27, 1965

House of Commons Procedures impartial Speaker who is not concerned about pressures being applied by members of the executive. Surely, Sir, the events of the past, and the very recent past-the year 1956 especially comes to mind-indicate that on certain occasions a Speaker who is a Government appointee and who must still look forward to a future and the prospect of further advancement within his own party can be forced to do things which he possibly considers would be in his best personal interests, but would not be in the best interests of parliament. As yet we have not had that kind of assurance from the Government, if they intend to appoint a permanent Speaker.
I have before me the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) in connection with the appointment of a permanent Speaker, with which he dealt in his remarks yesterday. He said this, among other things:
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
I am not quite sure what we mean by "permanent Speaker": there has been no definition, that I know of, of a permanent Speaker.
Later on on the same page he is reported
as having said:
But if we do that, and indeed if we do not, then whatever rules we make to increase the efficiency of the House and the better conduct of public business may not be as successful as we may like them to be; because it is important that the Speaker should not only be independent, but it should be obvious that he is independent and he should be freed from pressures against his independence.
I am afraid I do not have that kind of confidence at this time. I do not believe that the Speaker is completely independent and completely beyond the pressures of the executive. As a backbencher, and one who takes an active part in the debates of this House, I am very leery about accepting proposed changes until I am certain that there are no pressures which can be applied to the Speaker in respect of anything about which he has to make a judgment. Certainly we know that an individual filling the Speaker's position must endeavour to become impartial but, as I have already stated, it is not an independent position because the Speaker is appointed only for one parliament. He does not have that kind of independence which would relieve him from the uncertainty of ensuing elections.
If we are going to adopt rule changes which will greatly curtail our activities, with the understanding that parliament will be more efficient, then we as Members must be certain that the executive, who will be the beneficiaries, have no way of exerting influence in

respect of decisions arrived at by the Speaker. Surely there is only one way to accomplish that, and that is to name an individual-he may be elected by the Members of this House -and provide him with a constituency in respect of which all parties in the House agree not to contest. Such an individual must be certain that he can serve in that position for as many parliaments as he personally desires to remain Speaker, with that independence about which the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) spoke.
It is very nice for the Government to state that if we pass these rules it will give serious consideration to the appointment of a permanent Speaker. That is a very good and wonderful undertaking, but we have experienced many occasions during the past two years when promises have been made by the Prime Minister and Members of the Cabinet which were not followed by action. I do not think a better example of that situation can be found than the example set by the Government in respect of the position of the Union Jack as a flag of this nation. During that debate we were told that the Union Jack would be the flag of Canada under certain circumstances. From what I can gather now, it is only a flag of Canada under extremely rare and unique circumstances, and then only as far as Parliament Hill is concerned. It is flown nowhere else in an official capacity. That is a far different situation from that which the Government outlined when it proposed the dual flag resolution.
One cannot talk out of both sides of his mouth and expect hon. Members to have any confidence in what he is saying. It is one thing for the Prime Minister and Members of the Cabinet to suggest that we should pass these rule changes, at which time they will give serious consideration to the suggested appointment of a permanent Speaker, and quite another thing to have such a promise fulfilled, particularly when one remembers that the Prime Minister has said that he is not even sure what is meant by a "permanent Speaker".
