Before Your Honour puts the motion perhaps we should consider whether or not the motion itself is within the scope of the resolution now before the House, because we would not like to appear to be doing something which under the rules it is not possible to do. Under Section 44 of 22620-112
House of Commons Procedures the British North America Act, which is the constitution of Canada until it is changed, it is provided that:
The House of Commons on its first assembling after a general election shall proceed with all practicable speed to elect one of its members to be Speaker.
Now, that is something which we cannot change by a change in the rules of the House of Commons. This would require an amendment to the British North America Act. It would be my opinion, for what it is worth, that under the amendment to the British North America Act of 1949, this might be the kind of amendment that could be made by the Senate, the House of Commons and the Crown here in Canada. However, it would require an Act of Parliament to change that provision which is laid down for us in the constitution. I think the objective the hon. Member has in mind is laudable. Although we may quarrel about whether we use the word "permanent"-I do not like the word "permanent", I like the words the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) used, "continuing and independent". The word "permanent" suggests to me a sort of civil servant, someone who is not elected to this House or is elected in some phony way. I do not always agree with the right hon. gentleman opposite, but I do agree with what he stated the other day that the Speaker should be one of us, not someone chosen in some other way. This means he should be elected in a normal constituency, as is the case in the United Kingdom, and as the right hon. gentleman suggested ought to be the case here.
It seems to me it would not be within our power in this House alone to alter this condition. We could introduce a bill to change the British North America Act to provide for some other method of having a Speaker. I do not advance the other, technical ground that since the resolution before us deals with two points, limiting time for the consideration of Supply and allocating time for the consideration of other business, that this is beyond the scope of the resolution. I do not want to raise that kind of technicality. It seems to me that we are dealing with the rules. If the hon. gentleman were proposing something that was within the scope of the rules, something that this House alone could do without offending against the constitution, I would not want to be pedantic in raising an objection to it. I think we are trying co-operatively to do the best we can on this matter.
It is quite clear that under Article 44 of the British North America Act of 1867, which is
1748	COMMONS
House of Commons Procedures still the Constitution of Canada, this would be beyond the scope of the powers of this House. It was for this reason I asked the hon. gentleman a question before he moved his amendment. I have been wracking my brain, quite frankly, to think of another method by which we can achieve this objective, other than the method followed in the United Kingdom, which I think is a very good method. In the United Kingdom, the Speaker is elected just like any other Member. As I understand it, there is an understanding amongst the political parties-it is not part of the rules-that no regular, political party will oppose him. I think he has been opposed by independents two or three times recently. I would hope we could follow that British practice in our procedure. We would not attempt to try to write this into the rules or even try to amend the British North America Act, but that we would reach an understanding among ourselves through consultation. Yesterday the Prime Minister and today the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mac-Eachen) indicated the attitude of the Government toward this matter. The right hon. gentleman opposite indicated the attitude of the Opposition. I suggest that we could try this method.
Perhaps I am going beyond the point of order, Mr. Speaker, but perhaps the House will show the same tolerance that has been shown some other hon. Members. I suggest that we could deal with the matter in that broad way. Notwithstanding the hon. gentleman's great suspicion of our good faith, perhaps he could assume that on this occasion we really mean that we would like to see a good Speaker elected and re-elected, as long as his constituency wanted to elect him, and as long as he was satisfactory to the House, and that we would like to do anything practical to achieve that.
There is another section of the British North America Act, the preamble, which says our constitution should be the image, in its parliamentary aspects, of the British. I think this is one case where it would be good to follow it.

One of the most regrettable things that has happened in this debate was the initiation of the discussion of a permanent Speakership, and in a sense I believe that the Chair, early on in the debate, may have been at fault in allowing that particular part of the discussion to go so far. It is apparent, especially since personalities have been injected, that this is a potentially embarrassing situation. It points up the irrelevancy of the kind of discussion about these matters, because we have had mention of three particular persons.
We have something that is fairly concrete and clear before us, and discussion of a permanent Speaker has absolutely nothing to do with it. I not only suggest, Mr. Speaker, that you rule the amendment out of order but that you take it upon yourself, perhaps in consultation with your officials, to tighten up the whole discussion on whether we should have a permanent Speaker. The feelings of certain people are involved, and if you do not do this we are going to have a pretty bitter and disgraceful discussion in the House, because a great many of us are highly opinionated and prejudiced in this regard, particularly with regard to some of the personalities suggested.

speechtext:
My chief purpose in intervening in the debate at this stage is to introduce an amendment which, in the interest of real freedom of speech in this House, I consider essential, to the effective operation of the proposed order in respect to the allocation of time for debate. Before I introduce the amendment, however, Mr. Speaker, I would like-I hope without repeating what other Members have said- to make a few general observations. I have only been a Member of this House for three years, although I have been interested in its activities for many years, but from the very first moment I came here I have been deeply interested in the necessity for amendments of the rules of the House.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
I think it may well be that some new Members, like myself, coming from other walks of life and unfamiliar with all the details of parliamentary procedure and many of its traditions, tend to be too impatient with what they discover when they come into the House. But it seems to me there is equal danger that those who stay in the House for some time, because they are devoted to the House of Commons as an institution, may fail to take a sufficiently objective and critical look at its operations, and they sometimes put up with situations which, if they had not been here for some time, they would regard as intolerable.
It seems to me that this question of the reform of the procedure of parliament is not just a matter of the public image of parliament. We are all aware of the widespread public impression that parliament as an institution is at the moment in some disrepute. There is nothing particularly new about this.
I think in the whole history of the Mother of Parliaments, parliament has frequently been in disrepute. I acknowledge, as I think
1752	COMMONS
House of Commons Procedures has been said already in the debate, that this popular judgment is sometimes due to ignorance, sometimes due to an incomplete knowledge of the purpose and traditions of this House, and sometimes due to the quite inevitable circumstance that the less constructive aspects of our activities sometimes receive the greatest degree of public attention. But it is my view that there is a solid basis for the public's unhappiness with Parliament at the present time; and I am quite sure there is nothing we can do that will tend more to enhance the reputation of this historic institution than to improve, radically improve, the procedure which we have in the House.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, we in this party have made clear our determination to support the proposed changes before the House in principle; and in addition to that we are very pleased by the amendments which have been worked out through the collective judgment of some of the Members of the House. It is our view that, in spite of our reservations about some details, the proposed changes, so far from constituting an invasion of the rights of individual Members, if anything perhaps do not go far enough. We believe, moreover, that the changes proposed will not be the achievement of any one party or the Government, but will be the achievement of the constructive thinking of Members of all parties in this House. The important question I suggest, Mr. Speaker, is whether or not the procedural changes are, in our best judgment as Members of this House, likely to enable us to fulfil our functions more effectively in the interests of the people of this country of whom we are the servants.
Others in this debate have defined with more eloquence and learning than I can muster what are the functions of parliament; but for the purposes of my contribution I would like to mention three vital functions. The first is that we are the supreme legislative body in this country; and I do not think we should discount the importance of this function-I think it is of vital importance. It is true that in practice today most legislation is initiated by the Government, and that under our present system much of the drafting, and indeed many of the decisions about the legislation which is to be presented, is not decided by Members of the House, or even by the Cabinet, but by advisers from the civil service. It is also true that there has developed a modern habit of delegating legislative power and giving parliament only the

DEBATES	May 27, 1965
function of laying down general guide lines. By this system, important and operative details of legislation are reserved to Order in Council; but this seems to me to be an inevitable tendency and it is perhaps useless for us to complain about it.
Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, I believe that a far greater volume of legislation of a constructive nature should be scrutinized and could be improved by parliament if there were a reasonable streamlining of our procedure. The second function of parliament that I would like to mention is that it is a supreme forum for the public discussion of important issues, and indeed of some issues that may not appear to be very important to the Government. For this reason we must be careful, as has been said by several hon. Members already in this debate, not to abridge unduly the rights of the Opposition or interfere with freedom of speech in this chamber. However, it seems to me that allocation of time and the various matters coming before the House are absolutely essential to that orderly freedom of speech which is real freedom of speech.
There is no freedom of speech if a minority can, even after they have had the opportunity to express their point of view, prevent by prolonged discussion the majority of the House from dealing adequately, or even at all, with other issues. I have no doubt that the proposals that we are discussing for the allocation of time by majority vote, and following the approval of the representatives of the parties, will only be used very rarely; and I suggest that any government or any majority that abuses these rules for the allocation of time will be making a very grave political mistake, one that would be very dangerous to its own future. I have no doubt that most of the orderly arrangement of the business of the House that is required can be done with good sense and judgment at the level of the Business Committee.
I do not imagine there are any effective deliberative or legislative bodies anywhere in the world that do not have some provision limiting the time for debate. For this reason- and I respect the views of those who have spoken differently in this House-I suggest it is nonsense to claim that the proposals we have before us, amended and improved as I think they have been by discussion and by the amendments that have been approved by this House, are an invasion of any freedom of speech. I have spent some time myself being interested in the problem of trying to maintain what I believe to be freedom of
May 27, 1965	COMMONS
speech, but I have always understood that freedom of speech was freedom subject to reasonable regulation.
Another function of parliament is that it should be a check on the executive, a watchdog over the constitutional and judicial safeguards of personal freedom. In these days it is frequently said that the role of the individual Member has virtually withered away. Mr. R. H. S. Crossman, who is one of the outstanding ministers in the British Government and a parliamentarian of considerable experience, referred to the present jobs of a backbench member as "to obey the party Whips in the lobby whatever his conscience may say, to act as a kind of political welfare officer for his constituents, and by questions and speeches to ventilate the causes he believes in".
The hon. Member for Queens (Mr. Mac-quarrie), in his excellent contribution to this debate, spoke of the representative role of parliament and said that it is with this representative role that we must be concerned, and must watch carefully when anything happens to diminish the role of the spokesmen from all parts of the country, the backbenchers. It is my view that generally speaking the role of the backbench Members of all parties in all the functions of parliament, as legislators, as watchdogs of public expenditures and bureaucracy, our function as a forum for public discussion, can all be made more worth while and more effective by the adoption of the resolution that is before us. I know that some Members of this House are very sceptical about the efficiency of our committees system. I believe that the changes which are proposed will tend toward establishing a system in which backbench Members can make a real and more effective contribution.
However, Mr. Speaker-and I now come to the point of my amendment-the rights of backbenchers in every section of this House can be seriously interfered with if we proceed with the allocation of time for debate, which we have already approved as far as the amendments before the House are concerned, without any reduction at all in the time limit for individual speakers who sit in the House.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
In September 1964 we in this party put forward a number of proposals to improve, as we thought, the procedures of this House. One of the items was that it was necessary that there be further limitation of the time for speaking for individual Members, a greater
DEBATES	1753
House of Commons Procedures limitation than presently exists in Standing Order 31. The proposal made in the amendment which I will put forward is that if there is an order for time allocation made, either as the result of the recommendation of the Business Committee or as the result of an order of the House following upon a motion by a Member of the Government, then in either case the time for speaking for an individual Member should be limited to 20 minutes and the time for speeches by leaders, or those opening and replying to the debate, should be limited to 40 minutes.
The amendments which have been approved by the House regarding allocation of time for total debate provide for two days on second reading, two days in committee of the whole and one day on third reading. If we make no limitation whatever of the contribution an individual Member of the House can make, and if Standing Order 31 (1) remains in effect, then we could have a situation where the whole of the two days allocated to first and second readings of a given subject in this House could well be taken up by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), or by the Minister moving a Government order or a Member speaking in reply thereto.
I remind hon. Members of the House that the present Standing Order 31 (1) provides for unlimited time for certain Members of the House in certain circumstances. We all recognize the importance of giving special opportunities to address the House to those who have special responsibilities. However, I should like to point out that it is perfectly possible, if we do not adopt any limitation of time, to have debates in the House reduced to the point where we hear nothing but speeches from the leaders of the various parties in the House.
I for one, and perhaps other hon. Members too, recall that on one occasion, in fact the very first debate I heard in the House, the present Prime Minister spoke for three hours and the Leader of the Opposition spoke for almost three hours. I think that was in 1963, or it may have been in 1962. As far as I am concerned they were excellent 'speeches, but they would have been much better speeches had they been made in 40 minutes.
If the amendment I am proposing is adopted, some hon. Members in this House who are used to making 40 minute speeches would find that having to confine their remarks to 20 minutes would involve some selfdiscipline. It would also involve a great deal more preparation than would a longer speech.

Yes, if I am not interrupted any more. I am almost through. I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that the shortening of speeches in this House would be beneficial in itself because, as I have said, it would make for better speeches.
The real purpose of my speech tonight is not just to get shorter speeches, although I am sure that would be a real improvement in itself, but to give a reasonable opportunity to backbenchers or speakers from various parts of Canada representing various interests in Canada to be heard in debate, as a result of my proposed amendment. I do not want to see a reasonable allocation of time for total debate destroyed, as it would be as far as I am concerned, by giving unlimited time to individual debaters or by unnecessarily lengthy debate by individual Members. We do not want this House to become a debating chamber in which we have a series of speeches from those who hold positions of leadership in the House. I am not criticizing any of the leaders of the House; they are all interesting and excellent speakers. But I do not think our purpose is to come here and listen to speeches from leaders. I think our purpose is to come here to represent the people of Canada resident in the areas from which we come, regardless of where we happen to sit in this House. I am absolutely convinced that if at the same time as we adopted an allocation of time for total debate, we permitted under our rules some individual

Members unlimited time and others 40 minutes for purposes of debate, then we would not have representative debate in this House.
In my opinion the time allocation rule is necessary and I am prepared to support it. Mr. Speaker, regardless of how the present amendment is read, I promise to take no more than five minutes to make my remarks. I should first like to comment about the amendment now before us, and I believe that is all I am entitled to discuss at this time.
I am very encouraged by the progress we have been making in the House in respect of the proposed amendments, and the unanimity with which certain amendments have been accepted would indicate that this House is now prepared to give serious consideration to proposals designed to make the business of the House more effective.
The hon. Member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) has suggested in effect that there be a limitation of time placed on Members' speeches, including the speeches of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), during any debate which is subject to the time limitation. He may have a good idea in principle, which may be acceptable if it is changed substantially in one or two respects.
The first change relates to the suggestion made by the hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill), to the effect that the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Official Opposition are recognized officers of this House and have traditionally been given special consideration under the rules of this House. Perhaps the hon. Member's omission in this regard was an oversight, but that can and ought to be corrected.
The second change relates to the fact that he has failed to make a differentiation between the different kinds of debate which take place in the House. For example, we might be debating on second reading a very important bill, in respect of which the Prime Minister finds it necessary to outline the background material in some detail. Likewise, the Leader of the Opposition might find that there is a great deal of background leading up to certain events and proposals under discussion

CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION- RESOLUTION OF PROTEST FROM KNIGHTS OF COLUMBUS
speechtext:
Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, I put a question to the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne), in his capacity as minister responsible for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, a state-owned corporation which is in a poor state. I wanted to know whether he meant to take a stand in view of the many protests he is receiving from all sides.
A few days ago, the Supreme Council of the Knights of Columbus, while holding a convention in Ste. Adele, passed a resolution of protest against the C.B.C. from which I should like to quote a few excerpts:
It is resolved that a strong protest he made to the Secretary of State against the C.B.C.'s policy of allowing fellow-traveller leftists, agnostics, terrorists and other trouble-makers to promote, on certain programs, class struggles and contempt for religious, civil and legal authorities.
It is resolved that the federal government be asked to set up within the C.B.C. a censorship board to remove from the public networks programs which condone crime, violence, immorality in all its forms.
Mr. Speaker, the Order of the Knights of Columbus has in Canada more than 125,000 members who represent almost a million people and is recognized as a serious organization which fights for the respect and maintenance of order, understanding and common sense.
The taxpayers are simply asking for an answer from the Secretary of State. Will they get it? A few days previously, the magazine Aufourd'hui Quebec, a very dynamic and widely read publication, even if it is still quite young, published on the activities of the C.B.C. a detailed and well documented article entitled: A crown corporation in poor shape.
Mr. Gilles Dandurand, director of the magazine, begins his article by asking a question, and I quote:
To His Excellency Governor General Vanier, who is above Mr. Pearson;
To Prime Minister Pearson, who is above Mr. Maurice Lamontagne;
To Mr. Maurice Lamontagne, who is Mr. Ouimet's boss;
May 27, 1965	COMMONS
To federal members of Parliament-
And here is the question:
Are you aware that the C.B.C., a state Corporation, is in "bad shape"?
Will you keep on using the money we have honestly earned to finance "numerous T.V. programs bent on systematically and deliberately running down the highest principles of Christian faith and morals", as the bishops of Quebec stated on November 16, 1959?
During those six years, this "deliberate running down of the highest principles of Christian faith and morals" continues to be no less deliberate and more and more systematically organized... So...?
Those who are footing the bill are only asking you for an answer.
Is it asking too much?
Does the Secretary of State recall an article published in the newspaper Le Soleil last March 24 referring to a statement signed by 76,000 Canadian women, most of whom were mothers, and which read as follows:
We are asking our representatives to put an end to the control exercised by a minority over the C.B.C. to spread perversion, pornography, free love, blasphemy, use of drugs, violence and crime-
Mr. Secretary of State, those who pay are merely asking for an answer. Is it too much to ask?
Only a few days ago, Hon. Frederic Dorion, chief justice of the Quebec Superior Court, condemned television as being too often the best school of perversity and immorality. Speaking before a group of lawyers Judge Dorion said:
Unfortunately, I am also aware that all those attempts to keep order and protect morals are too often opposed by certain publicity media which, like television, frequently present programs so immoral and indecent that they stir up the indignation of decent viewers, especially fathers and mothers.
This communication medium which has now come into most of our homes and makes its way there by both word and picture, has become a need and an extraordinary means of propaganda. Whoever wishes to safeguard Christian principles which none the less are still the basis of our society, may but look at and listen to scenes we witness several times during the week, and he will realize that television is often the greatest school of perversion and immorality, particularly because it is introduced almost forcibly into our homes. For instance can the use of firearms be promoted without personal risks? Is it proper to show the feats and skill of bandits, to demonstrate so often the triumph of violence and fraud, even when it is helping justice, to show the indecency of beatniks and of eccentric girls who resort to provocative gestures?
Justice Dorion, a man in a position of authority, is well placed to see the nefarious effect television can have on our youth and on those who are not so young.
Many other people have protested to the C.B.C. and, in this house hon. members have, 22620-1131

TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY-NEW BRUNSWICK -PROPOSED CHANGE IN ROUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question which I posed to the Minister of Public Works this afternoon was inspired by a telegram received from the Bath Chamber of Commerce with reference to the routing of the Trans-Canada Highway between Florenceville and Perth, New Brunswick, and the decision which had been suggested to them as having been final as a result of the questions which they had put to the Government of New Brunswick-and the
May 27, 1965
1758	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion answers received-in spite of the fact that they had made a submission to the Minister stating this matter was of extreme importance to their district, involving expenditures in excess of several millions of dollars, and they were assured the question was under review by the Department here.
Their request was that before granting approval to the west side route, they felt the general public interest rendered it imperative that a top level official of the Department of Public Works be sent to evaluate that section of the highway both as to cost of construction and service to the public.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
In explanation I might say I think it would be of interest to the House to know that the suggestion that the highway be diverted to the west side of the river involves the crossing of the river and proceeding along the river to the village of Andover, which is exactly opposite Perth. This puts the highway through a corridor which, beginning at Crossville at a distance of seven or eight miles gradually lessens in width until at Perth it is probably several miles in length, as against the original plan to follow the river on the east side through the various built up towns, or villages might be the better description, of Florenceville, Bristol, Bath, Upper Kent, Kilburn, Perth, and so on.
The request made to the Minister is that a top level official of the Department be sent to investigate the situation. I am very conscious of the fact that bridges are necessary across the river at Florenceville and I have nothing against the building of a highway on the west side. Nevertheless, the built up part of the area is on the other side of the river and before a final decision is made I think the Minister should comply with the request made to him so that careful consideration is given to building this road through that part of the area in which the greatest number of people would be served along the route of the highway.
The western side of the Saint John River is just a corridor to the Maine border, as I said, whereas on the eastern side when you get down to Bristol you run into the road between Bristol and the village of Juniper, down the Miramichi to Newcastle and Chatham. It seems to me that the local needs of the public would best be served by carefully investigating the contention of the Bath Chamber of Commerce that a route on the east side of the river should be followed. This is a reasonable request. The Bath Cham-


ber of Commerce is certainly a non-partisan body with no interest except the general interest of the public. I hope the Minister will see his way clear to comply with it.
I should also call attention to the fact that on the east side of the river below Perth six or seven miles of the Trans-Canada highway have already been constructed. This paving would have to be abandoned if the route on the west side were adhered to. In the light of all these considerations it appears that to change the route to the western side of the river at this late date would not only be unduly expensive, involving a good many millions of dollars in extra expenditure, but that it would also result in inconvenience to the general public and to the traffic bound for the eastern side of the province.
Then there is the highway from Bristol to Newcastle, a route which as far as local interest is concerned is of tremendous importance. It seems to me that a request by an independent body such as the Bath Chamber of Commerce to the federal Minister should be given the consideration which I believe it merits. I believe that the building of the Trans-Canada highway on the eastern side of the river will develop the local community; it will take care of the local traffic; it will also take care of the traffic, as I have said, that is somewhat greater as far as volume is concerned and also so far as general destination is concerned. Then in regard to all these matters there is the question of cost. I believe investigation will show that the expenditure will be much greater-

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-BRITISH COLUMBIA-LOSSES SUFFERED BY FRUIT GROWERS
AGRICULTURE-BRITISH COLUMBIA-LOSSES SUFFERED BY FRUIT GROWERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after 40 years spent as a tree fruit grower in British Columbia, I am naturally well versed in the problems that face the tree fruit producers in that province and am sympathetic to their proposals. It was on that account and at the request of several persons that I inquired of the Minister what
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion was being done to assist these tree fruit producers at the present time. I must say, Mr. Speaker, with all due respect to the Chair, that I simply cannot understand why I was ruled out of order. I was simply inquiring of a Minister whether an investigation had been conducted and whether consideration was being given to amending the Farm Credit Corporation Act. However, I must take my medicine and stay here tonight, and I apologize to the hon. Member for Hull for keeping him so late out of bed.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
I asked the following question on the Orders of the Day today:
Has the Minister held an investigation of the circumstances that exist with respect to the losses suffered from frost by certain fruit growers in British Columbia this year? Is consideration being given to amendment to the Farm Credit Corporation Act to cover this unexpected and unfortunate situation?
I had some personal knowledge of this, Mr. Speaker.
The fruit growers of British Columbia are concerned with two problems at this time, in addition to many others. First is the unexpected frost damage caused to stone fruits in British Columbia this spring; the second is the necessity of changing certain varieties of fruit, apples in particular, because of change in tastes.
This subject was discussed at the annual convention of the British Columbia Fruit Growers Association held on January 19, 20 and 21, 1965. I am just going to mention briefly the resolution which was adopted by that convention. It was entitled: "Financial Assistance Program - Keremeos-Cawston'', which was the local which submitted it. The resolution reads:
Whereas there is no act or arrangement at present under which fruit growers may borrow long term, low interest funds to renovate their orchards by cutting out trees of low marketable varieties or on low volume rootstocks and replacing the removed trees with varieties acceptable to the consuming public and on high volume type rootstocks, and
Whereas many orchards were planted 30 to 40 years ago and the production has fallen to 500 to 700 bushels per acre of average to low quality fruit and are therefore uneconomical, and
Whereas it is estimated in the United States that production of 1500 bushels of high quality apples per acre must be produced in the years to come to meet competition
Therefore be it resolved that the British Columbia Fruit Growers Association approach the Canadian Government and request that the Farm Credit Corporation or other Government plan be amended to the extent that loans be made available to fruit farmers to enable them to cut out all or a part of their trees, if thought necessary, or replant with ac-
May 27, 1965
1760	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion ceptable market varieties on quick bearing high volume rootstocks, said loans to cover not only the removing of old trees and replanting of new ones, but the continued care and maintenance of the new trees until they have grown to an economic size, and moreover funds be loaned to take care of the livelihood of the farmer to enable him to carry out the above renovations.
That is one problem that has concerned them, particularly in recent years owing to changing market conditions. The other one which I mentioned before is the concern over the effects of frost on stone fruits grown in the southeastern portion of British Columbia.
I know the Minister is interested in the problem and is sympathetic to it, and that the officials of his department have been investigating both aspects of the problem as presented to the department by the British Columbia Fruit Growers Association.
It was on that account that I asked my question, because they are anxious to know whether the Government is giving consideration to amending the legislation or to providing some assistance with respect to the losses being incurred as a result of fruit damage this year.

am sure the hon. Member will accept the fact that all Members on this side of the House are really sorry for these growers in British

Columbia as a result of the fruit losses they have suffered this year. Such a matter as this is generally a matter for the Provincial Government, and we know that the Provincial Government is at the present time making a survey to assess the extent of the damage caused. Whenever they find it necessary they may come to the Federal Government for help and they will be well received.
In respect of the second point, the hon. Member spoke about an amendment to the law. I do not know whether or not it is the intention of the Government to propose an amendment this year, but I can assure him that the Farm Credit Corporation has been in close touch with the situation facing fruit growers in British Columbia. This matter was discussed today by the Chairman of the Corporation with the branch manager in British Columbia. Those borrowers who are unable to make payments to the Corporation without undue hardship, as a result of losses beyond their control, will be permitted to postpone the payment of their instalments. Consideration as to any future policies the Corporation may adopt must await a further and more detailed assessment of the situation which has developed.
